title: SN2 on a 2° halide: inversion

steps.label: Cyanide attacks the carbon from the back side as bromide leaves
steps.note: One concerted step: the nucleophile comes in opposite the C–Br bond, so the stereocenter inverts.

why: Cyanide is a strong nucleophile but a weak base, and DMSO is polar aprotic, so a 2° halide goes SN2. Backside attack inverts the stereocenter: (S)-2-bromobutane gives (R)-2-methylbutanenitrile.

traps.explains: That's retention, the (S) nitrile. SN2 is a backside attack, so the configuration inverts.
A racemic mixture comes from SN1 (a planar carbocation). A strong nucleophile in a polar aprotic solvent on a 2° carbon means SN2, a single inverted product.
Cyanide is a weak base, so it substitutes rather than eliminates. E2 needs a strong (often bulky) base.

title: SN2 on a 1° halide

steps.label: Azide attacks the CH2 carbon from the back side as bromide leaves
steps.note: Unhindered 1° carbon and a polar aprotic solvent: a fast, single-step SN2.

why: A 1° carbon is unhindered and cannot form a stable carbocation, so it reacts by SN2. Azide is a strong nucleophile but a weak base, and DMF (polar aprotic) leaves it unsolvated and reactive, so it does one-step backside attack on the carbon bearing Br.

traps.explains: Azide is a weak base and the 1° carbon is easy to reach, so substitution wins. E2 on a 1° halide needs a strong, bulky base such as KOtBu.
No carbocation forms on a 1° carbon, so there is no hydride shift. SN2 puts the nucleophile exactly where Br was.
That's the amine, which needs a second step (LiAlH4 or H2, Pd) to reduce the azide. Substitution alone gives the alkyl azide.

title: Solvolysis of a 3° halide: SN1

steps.label: The C–Br bond breaks on its own, leaving a 3° carbocation
steps.note: Slow, rate-determining step: only the substrate is involved, so the rate doesn't depend on ethanol.

steps.label: Ethanol's oxygen attacks the carbocation
steps.note: A weak, neutral nucleophile is fine here: the carbocation is very reactive.

steps.label: Another ethanol removes the proton from the oxonium ion
steps.note: The solvent acts as the base; the by-product is protonated ethanol (with Br⁻, i.e. HBr).

why: A 3° carbon is too crowded for backside attack but forms a stable 3° carbocation, and ethanol is a weak nucleophile in a protic solvent that stabilises ions, so the halide ionizes (SN1). Ethanol then adds to the planar cation and loses a proton to give the ether; without heat or a strong base, substitution beats elimination.

traps.explains: Elimination (E1) is only a minor side product here. With a weak base and no heat, the solvent mostly adds to the cation; strong base (E2) or heat (E1) would give the alkene.
The nucleophile is the solvent. In ethanol, ethanol adds to the cation; you'd get tert-butanol only in water.
Substitution happens at the carbon that lost Br, which carries the positive charge. Ethanol does not bond to a neighbouring CH3.

title: 3° halide + small strong base: E2, Zaitsev

steps.label: Ethoxide removes a β-H as the C=C forms and bromide leaves, all at once
steps.note: E2 is one concerted step. The H taken is on the more substituted β-carbon, giving the Zaitsev alkene.

why: A 3° halide can't do SN2, and ethoxide is a strong base, so E2 wins over SN1. Ethoxide is small, so it can reach the internal β-H and gives the more substituted (Zaitsev) alkene, here tetrasubstituted 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene.

traps.explains: That's the Hofmann (less substituted) alkene, which you get with a bulky base like KOtBu. Small ethoxide gives the more stable Zaitsev alkene.
A 3° carbon is too hindered for SN2 backside attack, and a strong base favours E2 over SN1. Substitution is at most minor.
There's no water or hydroxide here. Ethoxide acts as a base, and on a 3° halide it eliminates.

title: Bulky base: E2, Hofmann alkene

steps.label: tert-Butoxide removes a β-H from the CH3 group as the C=C forms and bromide leaves
steps.note: One concerted step. The bulky base reaches the exposed CH3 hydrogens, not the hindered CH, so the less substituted (Hofmann) alkene forms.

why: A 3° halide with a strong base goes E2. tert-Butoxide is bulky, so it pulls off the most accessible β-H on a CH3 group rather than the hindered internal one, giving the less substituted (Hofmann) alkene, 2,3-dimethylbut-1-ene.

traps.explains: That's the Zaitsev alkene, which a small base like ethoxide gives. The bulky tert-butoxide can't reach the internal β-H, so the less substituted alkene is major.
tert-Butoxide is far too bulky to act as a nucleophile, especially at a 3° carbon. It only acts as a base.
There's no water or hydroxide to substitute. Even the alcohol solvent (tBuOH) is a poor, bulky nucleophile; the strong bulky base eliminates.

title: 2° halide + strong base, heat: E2
why: On a 2° halide the deciding factor is the reagent: ethoxide is a strong base (unlike cyanide), and heat favours elimination, so E2 is major. The small base gives the Zaitsev alkene, and the trans (E) isomer is more stable than cis, so (E)-but-2-ene is the major product.

traps.explains: SN2 is only the minor path here. Ethoxide is a strong base and heat favours elimination; a weakly basic nucleophile like CN- or N3- in DMSO would substitute instead.
But-1-ene is the Hofmann product, major only with a bulky base like KOtBu. Small ethoxide gives the more substituted but-2-ene.
Both but-2-ene isomers form, but the trans (E) alkene is more stable and is the major product; cis (Z) is minor.

title: 3° alcohol + acid, heat: E1

steps.label: Sulfuric acid protonates the OH group
steps.note: OH⁻ is a poor leaving group; protonation turns it into water, a good one.

steps.label: Water leaves, giving a 3° carbocation
steps.note: Rate-determining step.

steps.label: Water removes a β-H next to the carbocation, forming the C=C
steps.note: Losing the H from the CH (not a CH3) gives the more substituted, Zaitsev alkene.

why: Strong acid protonates the OH into water, a good leaving group, and the 3° alcohol ionizes to a 3° carbocation (E1). With heat and only weak nucleophiles (H2O, HSO4-), a weak base removes a β-H, giving the more substituted (Zaitsev) alkene, 2-methylbut-2-ene.

traps.explains: That's the less substituted (Hofmann) alkene, only a minor product. E1 goes through a carbocation and gives the more stable, more substituted alkene.
Ether formation (another alcohol attacking the cation) needs milder conditions. Heat favours elimination, and the alkene distils out.
The sulfate is not the product. HSO4- is a very weak nucleophile; the cation loses a β-H instead, and heat drives off the alkene.

review: Key step shows the water that just left as the base; many texts use HSO4- instead. Either is acceptable.

title: SN1 at a stereocenter: racemization

steps.label: The C–Br bond breaks on its own, leaving a planar 3° carbocation
steps.note: The carbocation is sp2 and flat: the stereocenter is lost here.

steps.label: Water attacks the carbocation (from either face)
steps.note: Attack from the top or bottom face is about equally likely, so both enantiomers form.

steps.label: Another water removes a proton from the oxonium ion

why: A 3° halide with a weak nucleophile (water) in a protic solvent goes SN1. The leaving group departs first to give a planar carbocation, and water can add to either face, so (R)-3-bromo-3-methylhexane gives racemic 3-methylhexan-3-ol.

traps.explains: That's only the inverted (S) alcohol, the SN2 outcome. A 3° carbon can't do backside attack; the planar cation is attacked from both faces.
That's pure retention, the (R) alcohol. The leaving group is gone before water arrives, so neither face is preferred and both enantiomers form.
Elimination (E1) is a minor side product. With no strong base and no heat, the weak nucleophile mostly substitutes.

title: E2 is anti-periplanar: stereospecific alkene
why: Ethoxide is a strong base and heat favours elimination, so E2. E2 needs the β-H and Br anti-periplanar, and C2 has only one H, so only one conformation can react: in (1R,2R)-1-bromo-1,2-diphenylpropane that conformation puts the two phenyls on the same side, giving only (Z)-1,2-diphenylpropene.

traps.explains: (E)-1,2-Diphenylpropene comes from the (1R,2S) diastereomer. E2 is stereospecific: with the only β-H anti to Br, the phenyls in this isomer end up cis.
Ethoxide is a strong base, the carbon is 2° and hindered by two phenyls, and there is heat, so E2 beats SN2.
The H must come from the carbon next to C–Br (C2). The CH3 hydrogens are one carbon further away, so the double bond forms between C1 and C2.

review: Stereo derived with RDKit (3D embed, H–C2–C1–Br dihedral set to 180°): (1R,2R) gives the Z alkene (phenyls cis), (1R,2S) gives E. Please confirm against a textbook (McMurry discusses this example).

title: 2° benzylic halide in methanol: SN1

steps.label: The C–Br bond breaks, leaving a resonance-stabilized benzylic carbocation
steps.note: The positive charge is delocalized into the ring, which is why a 2° benzylic halide goes SN1.

steps.label: Methanol's oxygen attacks the carbocation
Another methanol removes the proton from the oxonium ion

why: A plain 2° halide in methanol reacts slowly, but this one is benzylic: losing Br- gives a carbocation stabilized by resonance into the ring. Methanol is a weak nucleophile and a protic solvent, so the reaction goes SN1, and methanol adds at the benzylic carbon to give the methyl ether.

traps.explains: Styrene would need a strong base (E2) or heat (E1). Methanol at room temperature is a weak base, so substitution dominates.
The positive charge is delocalized into the ring, but attack at the ring carbon would destroy aromaticity. The nucleophile adds at the benzylic carbon.
The nucleophile bonds to the carbon that lost Br (the cation carbon), not to the CH3 next to it.

title: 1° alcohol + PCC: aldehyde

steps.label: The alcohol oxygen attacks chromium; a Cr=O π bond moves onto oxygen
steps.note: Like a nucleophile adding to a C=O, but at chromium.

steps.label: Proton transfer from the oxonium oxygen to another oxygen on chromium
Pyridinium protonates the Cr–OH, making it a good leaving group
The Cr=O reforms and water leaves, giving the chromate ester
Pyridine removes the α-H; the C=O forms as the O–Cr bond breaks
steps.note: An E2-like elimination: chromium takes the electrons and is reduced from Cr(VI) to Cr(IV).

why: PCC is a mild chromium(VI) oxidant used without water (in CH2Cl2), so a 1° alcohol stops at the aldehyde: no water means no hydrate to oxidize further. The alcohol forms a chromate ester, then a base removes the C–H on the carbinol carbon as the O–Cr bond breaks, forming C=O. DMP and Swern oxidation do the same job.

traps.explains: Butanoic acid is the chromic acid (Jones) product. PCC works without water, so the aldehyde can't form a hydrate and isn't oxidized further.
Oxidation happens at the carbon that holds the OH, and no carbons move. A 1° alcohol gives an aldehyde; a ketone comes from a 2° alcohol.
PCC is an oxidant, not a dehydrating acid. Losing water to make an alkene needs strong acid and heat.

review: Key step drawn as pyridine removing the α-H from a chloro-chromate ester (RO–CrO2Cl) as Cr–O breaks; textbooks draw the ester and base differently. DMP and Swern are in the aliases as reagents giving the same product. Mechanism: chromate-ester formation drawn as attack at Cr, proton transfer, protonation by pyridinium, loss of water; courses vary a lot here (some show Cl⁻ leaving instead, or skip straight to the ester), so check it matches your course.

title: 1° alcohol + chromic acid: carboxylic acid

steps.label: The alcohol oxygen attacks chromium; a Cr=O π bond moves onto oxygen
Proton transfer from the oxonium oxygen to a Cr–OH
The Cr=O reforms and water leaves, giving the chromate ester
Water removes an α-H; C=O forms as the O–Cr bond breaks, giving the aldehyde
steps.note: With PCC (no water) the reaction stops here, at the aldehyde.

steps.label: Water adds to the aldehyde C=O
steps.note: The water in the chromic acid mixture turns the aldehyde into a hydrate, which can be oxidized again.

steps.label: Hydronium protonates the alkoxide oxygen
Water removes a proton from the other oxygen, giving the hydrate
A hydrate OH attacks a second chromic acid; a Cr=O π bond moves onto oxygen
Proton transfer from the oxonium oxygen to a Cr–OH
The Cr=O reforms and water leaves, giving a new chromate ester
Water removes the C–H; C=O forms as the O–Cr bond breaks, giving the carboxylic acid
steps.note: Same elimination as before; the carbon has now been oxidized twice.

why: Chromic acid is a strong Cr(VI) oxidant used in water. The 1° alcohol is first oxidized to the aldehyde, which adds water to form a hydrate (the key step shown); the hydrate is itself an alcohol, so it is oxidized again to the carboxylic acid.

traps.explains: Butanal is the PCC product. In aqueous chromic acid the aldehyde forms a hydrate and is oxidized on to the acid.
Oxidation happens at the carbon that holds the OH; no carbons move. A ketone comes from a 2° alcohol.
Chromic acid doesn't cleave C–C bonds of a simple alcohol, so the carbon count stays at four.

review: Key step chosen is hydrate formation (water adding to the intermediate aldehyde), the step that explains why chromic acid over-oxidizes and PCC doesn't. The chromate-ester steps are not drawn. Mechanism: each chromate-ester formation is drawn as attack at Cr, one intramolecular proton transfer, loss of water; hydrate formation is drawn as neutral water attack then proton transfers (to match the key step). Courses draw these parts differently, so check it matches your course.

title: 2° alcohol + chromic acid: ketone

steps.label: The alcohol oxygen attacks chromium; a Cr=O π bond moves onto oxygen
steps.note: Like a nucleophile adding to a C=O, but at chromium.

steps.label: Proton transfer from the oxonium oxygen to a Cr–OH
steps.note: In acid this is really two steps (deprotonate, then protonate) through the solvent.

steps.label: The Cr=O reforms and water leaves, giving the chromate ester
Water removes the H on the carbinol carbon; C=O forms as the O–Cr bond breaks
steps.note: An E2-like elimination: chromium takes the electrons and is reduced from Cr(VI) to Cr(IV).

why: A 2° alcohol has one H on the carbinol carbon, so oxidation gives a ketone. The alcohol forms a chromate ester, then water removes that C–H as the O–Cr bond breaks, making C=O. The ketone has no C–H left on the carbonyl carbon, so it isn't oxidized further.

traps.explains: Sulfuric acid is present, but chromic acid oxidizes the alcohol rather than dehydrating it. Dehydration to cyclohexene needs H2SO4 or H3PO4 with heat and no oxidant.
Chromic acid stops at the ketone: there is no H on the carbonyl carbon to remove. Ring cleavage to adipic acid needs much harsher oxidation (hot HNO3).
2° alcohols do oxidize. It's 3° alcohols, with no H on the carbinol carbon, that chromic acid can't oxidize.

review: Mechanism: chromate-ester formation drawn as attack at Cr, one proton transfer, loss of water; courses draw this part differently (some skip straight to the ester), so check it matches your course.

title: Alcohol + TsCl: tosylate, retention

steps.label: The alcohol oxygen attacks sulfur and chloride leaves
steps.note: The C–O bond is never touched, so the stereocenter keeps its configuration.

steps.label: Pyridine removes the proton from the oxygen
steps.note: Pyridine mops up the HCl so the solution doesn't become acidic.

why: The alcohol oxygen attacks sulfur and chloride leaves; pyridine mops up the HCl. The C–O bond of the stereocenter is never broken, so (R)-butan-2-ol gives the (R) tosylate with retention, now carrying a good leaving group.

traps.explains: That's the inverted (S) tosylate. The reaction happens at sulfur, so the C–O bond of the stereocenter is untouched and the configuration is retained.
Chloride leaves from sulfur and doesn't replace the OH. Making an alkyl chloride from an alcohol takes SOCl2.
Tosylation only installs a leaving group. Pyridine is a weak base and there is no heat, so no elimination happens in this step.

title: 2° alcohol + PBr3: bromide, inversion

steps.label: The alcohol oxygen attacks phosphorus and a bromide leaves
steps.note: This turns OH into an excellent leaving group (O–PBr2) without making a carbocation.

steps.label: Bromide attacks the carbon from the back side, displacing the oxygen group (SN2)
steps.note: Back-side attack: the stereocenter inverts.

why: PBr3 turns the OH into a good leaving group (O–PBr2), and the bromide released then attacks the carbon from the back in an SN2 step. No carbocation forms, so there is no rearrangement and the stereocenter inverts: (R)-butan-2-ol gives (S)-2-bromobutane.

traps.explains: That's retention, the (R) bromide. The C–O bond breaks in an SN2 step, so bromide comes in from the back and the configuration inverts.
A racemic product needs a carbocation (SN1, as with HBr on a 3° alcohol). PBr3 works by SN2, giving one inverted enantiomer.
Bromide is a weak base, and there is no heat, so the activated alcohol is substituted, not eliminated.

review: Mechanism: SN2 step drawn on the protonated R–O(H)–PBr2 (Klein-style, leaving group HOPBr2); the key step shows the deprotonated ROPBr2, as some texts do. The arrows are the same.

title: 1° alcohol + SOCl2: alkyl chloride

steps.label: The alcohol oxygen attacks sulfur and a chloride leaves
steps.note: This turns OH into a chlorosulfite, an excellent leaving group.

steps.label: Pyridine removes the proton from the oxygen
Chloride attacks the carbon from the back side, displacing the chlorosulfite (SN2)
steps.note: The leaving group falls apart into SO2 and Cl⁻, which drives the reaction.

why: SOCl2 converts the OH into a chlorosulfite, an excellent leaving group that falls apart into SO2 and Cl-. Chloride then attacks the unhindered 1° carbon in an SN2 step, so there is no carbocation and no rearrangement.

traps.explains: No carbocation forms on a 1° carbon, so there is no hydride shift. Chloride replaces the leaving group on the same carbon.
Pyridine is only a weak base that traps HCl; with a 1° carbon and no strong base, substitution wins over elimination.
SOCl2 is not an oxidant. Don't confuse it with the Swern oxidation, which uses oxalyl chloride and DMSO.

review: Mechanism: attack at S drawn as one concerted displacement of Cl⁻ (some texts show S=O addition then loss of Cl⁻ as two steps).

title: Williamson ether synthesis: pick the right pairing

steps.label: Hydride removes the O–H proton, giving the alkoxide
steps.note: H2 gas bubbles off, so this step is irreversible.

steps.label: The alkoxide attacks the methyl carbon and iodide leaves (SN2)
steps.note: SN2 at an unhindered CH3; the bulky alkoxide is fine as the nucleophile.

why: The Williamson synthesis is SN2, so the halide must be methyl or 1°. NaH turns tert-butanol into tert-butoxide, which attacks unhindered CH3I to give tert-butyl methyl ether. The other pairing (CH3O- with tert-butyl bromide) fails: a 3° halide with a strong base gives E2.

traps.explains: Isobutylene is what the wrong pairing gives: methoxide plus a 3° halide eliminates (E2). Here the halide is CH3I, which has no β-H and can only be substituted.
Only one tert-butyl group is present. CH3I supplies the second group, so the ether is tert-butyl methyl ether.
The O–H isn't replaced by iodide; that would need HI. NaH makes an alkoxide, which is the nucleophile that attacks CH3I.

title: Epoxide + acid/alcohol: more substituted carbon

steps.label: The acid protonates the epoxide oxygen
steps.note: Protonated methanol (from CH3OH + H2SO4) is the acid in the flask.

steps.label: Methanol attacks the more substituted carbon as the C–O bond breaks
steps.note: The more substituted C–O bond is weaker and that carbon carries more δ+, so it is attacked.

steps.label: Methanol removes the proton from the oxonium ion
steps.note: The acid is regenerated: it is a catalyst.

why: Acid protonates the epoxide oxygen, and the C–O bond to the more substituted carbon weakens most because that carbon carries more of the positive charge (SN1-like). Methanol, a weak nucleophile, attacks that 3° carbon from the back (anti to the O), giving 2-methoxy-2-methylpropan-1-ol.

traps.explains: That's the base-opening product. Under basic conditions the nucleophile hits the less hindered CH2; under acid it attacks the more substituted carbon that holds more positive charge.
Methanol is the solvent and the nucleophile here. A diol would need water as the nucleophile.
Opening the epoxide uses one methanol. The new alcohol is a poor leaving group and isn't replaced under these conditions.

title: Epoxide + alkoxide: less substituted carbon

steps.label: Methoxide attacks the less hindered CH2 carbon and the ring opens (SN2)
steps.note: A strong nucleophile with no acid follows SN2 rules: least hindered carbon.

steps.label: Workup: water protonates the alkoxide

why: Methoxide is a strong nucleophile, and the ring strain lets the epoxide O act as a leaving group without acid. The reaction is SN2, so methoxide attacks the less hindered CH2 carbon, and workup protonates the alkoxide to give 1-methoxy-2-methylpropan-2-ol.

traps.explains: That's the acid-catalysed product. Without acid, the strong nucleophile does SN2 at the less hindered carbon, not the more substituted one.
Methoxide is the nucleophile, so it ends up in the product. Workup water only protonates the alkoxide.
Methoxide opens the strained ring by substitution; it doesn't remove a proton to make an alkene.
